According to the 2026 Wet Season Agricultural Performance Survey (APS) conducted by the National Agricultural Extension and Research Liaison Services (NAERLS), Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, the projection covers four major cereal crops of maize, rice, sorghum and millet, with maize expected to account for the largest share of national production.
The survey which was released in Abuja on Wednesday, puts maize production at 11.67 million metric tonnes, rice at 9.63 million metric tonnes, sorghum at 6.55 million metric tonnes and millet at 1.54 million metric tonnes.
It also projects cassava production at 66.73 million metric tonnes and yam at 57.02 million metric tonnes in 2026.
Groundnut production is estimated at 5.41 million metric tonnes, while cowpea is projected at 4.46 million metric tonnes. Plantain and banana output is expected to reach 3.61 million metric tonnes, while soybean production is forecast at 956,744.7 metric tonnes.
Other projected outputs include onion at 1.38 million metric tonnes, ginger at 492,507.2 metric tonnes and cotton at 325,032.1 metric tonnes.
The survey also projects improvements in the yields of several crops compared with their 2025 levels. Sesame yield is expected to increase by 4.72 per cent, cowpea by 4.45 per cent, groundnut by 4.34 per cent and cotton by 3.88 per cent.
Maize yield is projected to rise by 2.96 per cent, from 2.26 metric tonnes per hectare in 2025 to 2.32 metric tonnes per hectare in 2026. Rice yield is expected to increase by 1.80 per cent, from 2.02 to 2.06 metric tonnes per hectare, while sorghum is projected to record a 0.65 per cent increase.
However, soybean yield is forecast to decline by 2.65 per cent, from 0.95 to 0.92 metric tonnes per hectare. Millet yield is expected to fall by 0.62 per cent, while cocoyam and ginger are projected to record marginal declines of 0.53 per cent and 0.07 per cent respectively.
The survey estimates ginger production at 492,507.2 metric tonnes, representing a 5.94 per cent decline. Kaduna State accounts for 62.1 per cent of the projected national output.
It identified access to clean planting materials as the leading requirement for ginger recovery, accounting for 28.8 per cent of responses from 400 respondents. Extension training accounted for 22 per cent.
On production risks, the report recorded severe flooding in Niger, Jigawa, Yobe, Ogun, Osun, Anambra and Ebonyi states, while Kaduna, Nasarawa, Benue and several southern states experienced moderate flooding.
Fall armyworm outbreaks were also reported as a threat to maize production, with severe infestations recorded in Kano and Taraba states.
The survey identified high input costs, irregular supplies of fertilisers and improved seeds, limited mechanisation, inadequate irrigation infrastructure and weak agricultural extension services among the major challenges affecting crop production.
On extension services, Sokoto recorded 1,116 unfilled positions against 109 staff in post. Gombe had 819 vacancies against 83 personnel, while Kebbi recorded 485 unfilled positions against 15 staff.
Across 15 reporting states, the survey put the extension agent-to-farm-family ratio at one to 4,982, with 2,064 active extension agents serving 10.28 million farm families.
Presenting the result, NAERLS executive director, Prof. Yusuf Sani recommended improved access to quality seeds, fertilisers, crop-protection products and seasonal finance, alongside investments in irrigation, mechanisation, agricultural research and extension services.
He also called for improved storage, processing, cold-chain facilities, transportation and market linkages to reduce post-harvest losses.
The survey further recommended institutionalising wet and dry season agricultural performance surveys as part of a continuous national agricultural monitoring system.
Reacting to the report, the Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Abubakar Kyari, commended NAERLS for the survey but called for improvements in the presentation of national production data, particularly historical comparisons.
The minister also urged NAERLS to strengthen its reporting of dry-season agricultural activities to complement the wet-season survey, noting that the federal government was promoting year-round farming.
He said the agency should begin preparations for the dry-season assessment, adding that the 2025 dry-season report should be presented by June.
Although the 2026 production figures are forecasts, it remain subject to harvest verification.
